title.en: Cari and Zapana: The Two Lords of the Collao
title.zh: 卡里與薩帕納:科利亞奧二主之爭

region.en: Hatun-colla and Chucuito, Lake Titicaca (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 的的喀喀湖畔哈通-科利亞與丘庫伊托(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Written by Cieza de León, publ. Markham trans. 1883 (Second Part)

source.work: Pedro de Cieza de León, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, trans. and ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1883

summary.en: In the reign of Inca Viracocha a lord named Zapana ruled over Hatun-colla. In the lake of Titicaca there are islands inhabited by people with large balsas, and another lord named Cari went to the islands, where he fought with the people in great battles out of which the Cari came forth a conqueror - with no other object than to destroy the villagers and carry off plunder. He returned to Chucuito, where he had established himself, and had under his sway the towns of Ylave, Yuli, Zepita, Pomata, and others. With the people he could collect, after having offered up great sacrifices to his gods, he marched against the Canas and defeated them; another victory at Luracachi made him very proud. When Zapana, the lord of Hatun-colla, heard of it he assembled his friends and vassals to despoil Cari, but Cari understood the design and retired in good order to Chucuito by an unfrequented road. Each chief, desiring the friendship of the Incas, sent ambassadors to Cuzco with great presents to secure Viracocha's alliance against the other.
summary.zh: 印加·維拉科查在位時,一位名叫薩帕納的領主統治哈通-科利亞。的的喀喀湖中有島嶼,住著乘大型蘆筏的人民;另一位名為卡里的領主赴島作戰,大戰連連,終為勝者——但其目的不過是屠村掠財。他凱旋回到自己經營的丘庫伊托,治下有伊拉維、尤利、塞皮塔、波馬塔等鎮。祭過神靈之後,他聚眾進攻卡納斯人,大敗之;又在盧拉卡奇獲勝,日益驕橫。哈通-科利亞之主薩帕納聞訊大怒,聚友邦與藩屬欲掠卡里;卡里識破其謀,循僻徑安然退回丘庫伊托。兩雄皆欲結好印加,便各攜重禮遣使庫斯科,求維拉科查聯盟以伐對方。

sensitivity.note: Pre-Inca Collao power politics preserved by Cieza's Orejone informants; the war opened the road to Inca domination of the lake.

passages.text: In the lake of Titicaca there are islands inhabited by people with large balsas, and another lord named Cari went to the islands, where he fought with the people insomuch that there were great battles between them, out of which the Cari came forth a conqueror. But he had no other object than to destroy the villagers and carry off plunder, without troubling himself to take prisoners. He returned to Chucuito, where he had established himself, and he had under his sway the towns of Ylave, Yuli, Zepita, Pomata, and others.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: With the people he could collect, after having offered up great sacrifices to his gods, he determined to march to the province of the Canas. These men, when they heard of his approach, assembled together, came forth to meet him, and fought a battle in which they were defeated with much loss. After this victory Cari determined to continue his advance, and arrived at Luracachi, where it is said that he fought another battle, and was equally fortunate. With these victories Cari became very proud.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Zapana, the lord of Hatun-colla, heard of it, he was very sad, and he assembled his friends and vassals to take the field and despoil Cari. But he could not do this so secretly as to prevent Cari from understanding the design of Zapana, and he retired in good order to Chucuito by an unfrequented road... And as the valour of the Incas, and the great power of Viracocha was spread abroad over all that region, each of these chiefs, desiring to obtain his friendship, sent ambassadors to Cuzco to secure his alliance and induce him to take part against the rival chief.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru (Hakluyt Society, 1883)

title.en: Chin in Breast, Voice Loud: How the Oracles Were Consulted
title.zh: 垂首含胸、高聲傳話:神諭的問法

region.en: Temples of the Andes and the coast (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 安第斯與海岸諸廟(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Written by Cieza de León, publ. Markham trans. 1883 (Second Part)

source.work: Pedro de Cieza de León, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, trans. and ed. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1883

summary.en: When the Inca determined to seek for an answer from the oracles, he sent for those who were accustomed to manage those things. The reply is sought by the priests in front of the idols: they bow down their shoulders, put their chins into their breasts, and begin to speak in loud voices. Occasionally I myself, with my own ears, have heard the Indians converse with the devil: in the province of Cartagena I heard the devil answer in a clear whistle, so loudly that a Christian more than half a league away heard the same whistle and was dismayed. On another day the Indians made great shoutings, publishing the reply of the devil. In some parts of these lands where they keep the dead in hammocks, the devils occasionally enter into the bodies and give answers: I heard a man named Aranda say that, in the island of Carex, he also saw one of these dead bodies speak, and the lies and nonsense they utter are laughable.
summary.zh: 印加王欲求神諭,便召慣司此事之人。祭司在偶像前求答:垂肩俯首,下巴抵胸,高聲傳話。塞薩自述:「我屢屢親耳聽過印第安人與魔鬼交談。」在卡塔赫納省的海港城巴亞伊雷,他聽見魔鬼以清晰口哨作答,聲聞半萊格之外,令一位在場基督徒惶然失措;另一日,印第安人高聲喧呼,宣告魔鬼的回復。在某些地方,人們把死者安置於吊床之中,魔鬼偶爾附體作答——有人名阿蘭達者說,他在卡雷克斯島親見一具死者屍體開口說話;那些謊言與胡話,聽來簡直可笑。

sensitivity.note: Cieza's rare first-person description of an oracle procedure (posture, voice, possession of hammock-kept dead); 'devil' is his frame, the procedure is the datum.

passages.text: This is done by the priests in front of the idols. They bow down their shoulders, put their chins into their breasts, and begin to speak in loud voices. Occasionally I myself, with my own ears, have heard the Indians converse with the devil.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: In some parts of these lands where they keep the dead in hammocks, the devils occasionally enter into the bodies and give answers. I heard a man named Aranda say that, in the island of Carex, he also saw one of these dead bodies speak, and the lies and nonsense they utter are laughable.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Inca determined to seek for an answer from the oracles, he sent for those who were accustomed to manage those things, and they say that the reply was that he should arrange to go to the Collao and seek the alliance of Cari.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cieza de León, Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru, ch. 41 (Markham 1883); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, The Second Part of the Chronicle of Peru (Hakluyt Society, 1883)

title.en: The Dinner of the Sun: Clay Cups Replaced with Gold
title.zh: 日神的晚餐:陶杯換金器

region.en: Coricancha, House of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽之屋科里坎查(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 36, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: After Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui had conquered the lands mentioned above and had triumphed over them, he came to visit the House of the Sun and the Mama-cunas or nuns who were there. He assisted one day to see how the Mama-cunas served the dinner of the Sun. This was to offer much richly cooked food to the image or idol of the Sun, and then to put it into a great fire on an altar. The same order was taken with the liquor: the chief of the Mama-cunas saluted the Sun with a small vase, and the rest was thrown on the fire; besides this many jars full of that liquor were poured into a trough which had a drain, all being offerings to the Sun. This service was performed with vessels of clay. As Pachacuti considered that the material of the vases was too poor, he presented very complete sets of vases of gold and silver for all the service that was necessary. To adorn the house more richly he caused a plate of fine gold to be made, two palmas broad and the length of the court-yard, and ordered it to be nailed high up on the wall in the manner of a cornice, passing all round the court-yard. This border or cornice of gold remained there down to the time of the Spaniards.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪征服諸邦、凱旋之後,親臨太陽之屋,查看瑪瑪庫納(貞女)侍奉日神晚餐的情形:眾女將精緻烹調的膳食供奉於太陽神像之前,然後投入祭壇上的烈火之中;酒漿亦然——瑪瑪庫納之首以小杯敬日神,其餘盡焚於火;此外又將滿罐奇恰酒傾入帶排水道的溝槽,盡為日神之祭。這些侍奉原用陶器。帕查庫提嫌器物卑陋,便賜下成套金銀器皿,以供全部所需。為使神屋更加輝煌,他又命人打造一塊兩掌寬、與庭院等長的純金薄板,釘於高牆之上作為簷飾,環繞庭院一周。這道金簷一直留存到西班牙人到來之日。

sensitivity.note: The daily liturgy of the Sun's meal as witnessed by the king; the gold cornice is the Coricancha's famous feature.

title.en: Sixteen Visitors and the Road from Quito to Chile
title.zh: 十六位巡察使與從基多到智利的大道

region.en: Roads of the empire, Quito to Chile (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 帝國大道:基多至智利(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 45, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Seeing that the people were in greater fear at beholding the valour of Tupac Inca, Pachacuti determined to have a visitation of the land, and nominated 16 visitors, four for each of the four suyus or divisions of the empire: Cunti-suyu from Cuzco south and west as far as the South Sea, Chinchay-suyu from Cuzco to the north and west, Anti-suyu from Cuzco to the east, and Colla-suyu from Cuzco to the south. These visitors inspected, before all things, the work of the tucuyricos and the methods of their government; they caused irrigating channels to be constructed for the crops, broke up land where this had been neglected, built andenes or cultivated terraces, and took up pastures for the Sun, the Inca, and Cuzco; above all they imposed very heavy tribute on all the produce. The visitations occupied two years; when they were completed the visitors returned to Cuzco, bringing with them certain cloths descriptive of the provinces they had visited, and reported fully to the Inca all that they had found and done. The Inca also despatched other orejones as overseers to make roads and hospices on the routes of the Inca: they made roads, now called 'of the Inca', over the mountains and along the sea coast; those on the sea coast are all provided, at the sides, with high walls of adobe, wherever it was possible to build them. These roads go from Quito to Chile, and into the forests of the Andes.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提見民眾愈發畏懼圖帕克·印加之勇武,便決意巡查全境,任命十六位巡察使——四蘇尤各四位:昆蒂蘇尤(自庫斯科向南向西直至南海)、欽查蘇尤(向北向西)、安蒂蘇尤(向東)、科利亞蘇尤(向南)。巡察使首先督察各處「圖庫里科」官長的施政;又主持修築灌溉渠、墾闢荒田、建造安第斯梯田,並為太陽、印加與庫斯科劃定牧場;尤以加征重貢於一切出產為最。巡查歷時兩年;事畢,巡察使攜記述各省的彩布返回庫斯科,向印加王詳細復命。印加王另遣耳垂貴胄為監工,沿王路修築道路與驛館——即今所稱「印加道」——越山嶺、沿海岸;海岸一路,凡可築處皆以土坯砌高牆護道兩側。這些道路自基多直達智利,並深入安第斯森林。

sensitivity.note: The imperial visitation as administrative myth-history; the painted cloth reports echo the Pachacuti annals-library record.

They caused irrigating channels to be constructed for the crops, broke up land where this had been neglected, built andenes or cultivated terraces, and took up pastures for the Sun, the Inca, and Cuzco.

title.en: 'O Father, Now Take Rest': The Obsequies of Pachacuti
title.zh: 「父王安息吧」:帕查庫提的葬禮

region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 48, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: When Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui died, two orejones were deputed to watch the body, and to allow no one to enter or go out to spread the news of his death, until orders had been given. The other Incas and orejones went with Tupac Inca to the House of the Sun and then ordered the twelve captains of the ayllus of the Inca's guard to come. They came with 2200 men of the guard, fully armed, and surrounded the Yupanqui with the fringe, and gave him the other insignia of sovereignty, as he had now inherited and succeeded his father. Taking him in the midst of themselves and of the guards, they escorted him to the great square, where he was seated, in majesty, on a superb throne. All the people of the city were then ordered to come and make obeisance to the Inca on pain of death. Those who had come with the Inca went to their houses to fetch presents to show reverence and do homage to the new Inca; he remained with his guards only until they returned with presents, doing homage and adoring. This having been done, they approached the Inca and said: 'O Sovereign Inca! O Father! now take rest.' At these words Tupac Inca showed much sadness and covered his head with his mantle, which they call llacolla. He next went, with all his company, to the place where the body of his father was laid, and there he put on mourning. All things were then arranged for the obsequies, and Tupac Inca Yupanqui did everything that his father had ordered at the point of death.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪駕崩後,兩名耳垂貴胄奉命看守遺體:未奉諭旨,任何人不得出入、不得走漏死訊。其餘印加貴胄隨圖帕克·印加前往太陽之屋,召王之衛隊十二世系的隊長;他們率兩千二百名全副武裝的衛士趕到,為戴王纓的尤潘琪呈上其餘王權印信——蓋他已承襲父位。眾人將他簇擁於衛隊中央,護送至大廣場,威嚴地安置在華麗御座之上;旋即傳令全城百姓前來朝拜新王,違者處死。隨王前來之人各自回宅取獻禮,以示尊崇;新王獨留衛隊之中,待眾人攜禮而返,行禮致敬,一一祭拜。禮成之後,眾人趨前說道:「至尊的印加王!父王!如今請安息吧。」聞言,圖帕克·印加面現哀戚,以名為「利亞科利亞」的方氅掩面。繼而,他率全體扈從前往父親遺體安放之所,披麻戴孝。喪儀諸事一一安排;圖帕克·印加·尤潘琪遵照父王臨終遺命,辦理後事,無所遺漏。

sensitivity.note: Accession-by-obsequies: the new king crowned before the death news escapes; the formula 'now take rest' marks the transfer of care.
